**Designing the Webtoon Viewer**

I'm making headway on the webtoon viewer. Right now, clicking a webtoon on the Home or Unlimited pages doesn't do anything specific. My goal is to add a new route and components to support actual webtoon viewing. I'll need to figure out what data to pass to the viewer and how to structure the episode navigation.


**Implementing the Viewer Component**

I'm currently working on the Viewer Component. I've decided to display the webtoon's title, an episode selector, and the content which will simulate episode images. Next, I plan to add the previous/next navigation buttons.


**Finalizing Viewer Navigation**

I'm now integrating the viewer navigation. I'll leverage `TOONS` for metadata. Instead of real images, I'm using placeholder images to simulate scrolling. I'm also implementing the episode selector at the top and the "Next Episode" and "Previous Episode" buttons at the bottom, per the user's feedback. I'm focusing on ensuring these elements are functional and provide a smooth user experience within the viewer.


**Defining Viewer UI Elements**

I'm currently finalizing the UI. I've decided on a clear title header, an episode selection mechanism – initially a horizontal scrollable list of buttons representing each episode. Below will be the image viewer area, and bottom navigation controls. I'm focusing on ensuring smooth, efficient navigation. I'm also updating WebtoonCard and WebtoonListItem to link to the new viewer route. I've chosen to use the existing mock image for now, and I will replace it with the webtoon image later.


**Developing the UI Elements**

I'm now fully immersed in the coding. I'm focusing on defining the header with the webtoon title. Then I'm working on an episode selector using buttons "1화," "2화," etc. (mocking 10 episodes for now). I'll also add a vertical flex container containing image tags that use the webtoon's cover, repeating it a few times to simulate the strip, as the text of the design description appears to suggest the reader be shown the full webtoon. Lastly, I'm integrating the footer navigation with "이전화" (Previous) and "다음화" (Next) buttons.


**Building Episode Navigation Logic**

I'm now focusing on implementing the episode navigation logic within the viewer. I've integrated `useNavigate` from `react-router-dom` to dynamically update the URL based on the current episode. I'm also ensuring the "Previous" and "Next" buttons work correctly, incrementing and decrementing the `currentEpisode` state. Additionally, the component now handles edge cases, such as when the first or last episode is displayed, preventing the episode count from going below 1 or exceeding `totalEpisodes`. To provide a smooth user experience, when the user navigates between episodes, the screen will always return to the top of the webpage.


**Refining the Episode Selector**

I've revised the episode selector to enhance its user-friendliness. The selector is now a horizontal, scrollable list of buttons, each representing an episode. Active episode buttons have a distinct style, contrasting the inactive ones. The component now uses `window.scrollTo(0, 0)` for each button click to ensure the user returns to the top of the webpage.

**Constructing Webtoon Strip**

I'm now integrating the webtoon's visual content. I've successfully incorporated the webtoon thumbnail image, repeating it multiple times to simulate the long-form strip format commonly used in webtoons. To create the visual separation between the images, I've added a black divider between each. Now, I'm focusing on ensuring this layout is responsive and presents the webtoon in an engaging manner.


**Enhancing Viewer Navigation**

I'm currently finalizing the navigation within the viewer component. I've integrated buttons for "다음화" (Next) and "목록으로 돌아가기" (Back to List), alongside a disabled state for the "Next" button when the current episode is the last.  I also incorporated a list navigation button that leverages the react-router-dom navigate prop.  My goal is to make sure the user can go from an episode to the next, as well as the ability to go back to the list of available webtoons.


**Implementing Responsive Webtoon Display**

I've just added the links to the `WebtoonCard` and `WebtoonListItem` components using `react-router-dom`'s `Link`, enabling navigation to individual webtoons. I'm now thinking about the viewer's layout. It will cover the full width or a good max-width. Also, I need to make the header sticky for easy navigation and to make the background dark to improve readability. I also need to update my mocks to reflect the `WebtoonCard` and `WebtoonListItem` changes.

1.  **뷰어 컴포넌트 생성 (`components/WebtoonViewer.tsx`)**: 상단에 에피소드 선택바, 중앙에 이미지(예시 데이터), 하단에 이전화/다음화 내비게이션을 배치합니다.

**Optimizing UI Integration**

My goal is to make a smooth and responsive interface, where the user knows where they are in the episode sequence. I'm currently checking for any edge cases.


**Adjusting Button States**

I'm currently focused on the button states for navigation. I've updated the "Previous" button to disable when `currentEpisode` is 0. Also, the "Next" button correctly disables when `currentEpisode` equals `totalEpisodes`. These ensure the user cannot go beyond the episode boundaries. The goal is a clean and intuitive navigation flow.


**Implementing Return Button**

I'm now integrating a "Return to List" button. It's designed to provide an easy way to exit the webtoon viewer and go back to the episode list. I'm currently focused on defining the exact scope of this project, specifically for a centered modal or popup for user registration triggered by a "Sign Up" button. **Refining the UI Elements**

I see a promotional banner, SNS login options, and an email sign-up form. There will be terms and conditions to acknowledge, a close button, and a "Free Sign Up" CTA. The "회원가입" button within the `Header` component triggers the modal. It will need a `SignUpModal` component.


**Conceptualizing Component Logic**

I'm now thinking about the logic and state management. The `Header.tsx` file will handle the `isSignUpOpen` state to control modal visibility. I'll pass an `onClose` function to the modal. It will need to close itself. I'm focusing on the structural foundation.


**Developing Modal Components**

I'm now focusing on the components of the modal itself, looking at input fields, the CTA button, and the checkbox area with "Agree to all" and individual options. I'm importing `SignUpModal` into `Header.tsx` and adding the state logic. The `회원가입` button now triggers the modal. I'm designing the modal, ensuring it works in both light and dark modes, with a promo banner.


**Analyzing Visual Styles**

I'm now analyzing the visual styling of the modal, looking at the input fields with standard Tailwind styling. I have decided to set brand-consistent colors. For the main CTA button, I'm choosing the Arata Green for consistency, but will copy the layout of the user's reference, making the text bold. The Naver, Kakao, Facebook, and Google colors are set.


**Constructing UI Elements**

I'm now thinking about the form inputs, including Email and Password fields. I've also outlined the checkboxes, including "전체 동의" and others. I'll implement basic state logic for these, particularly for the "All" checkbox. For a UI mockup, I'll focus on visual feedback instead of full validation. I'll implement a state to toggle it.

I'll update the `Header.tsx` file, by wiring up the button and verifying z-index values to ensure modal visibility above other elements. The reference image also needs attention, where a placeholder image or a gradient will be used to simulate the promo feeling, instead of external images. The SNS buttons will be rounded, and the form will have a divider to show "이메일 회원가입". Finally, I will construct final code.


**Adjusting Modal Responsiveness**

**Considering Alternative UX**

I'm now thinking about the desktop header. The user's request centers around the mobile experience, but I'm considering adding a "Sign Up" or "Login" button to the desktop version for better UX. I'll stick to the core scope, which implies a "Join Member" button, but I'll add the modal markup. I will style this exactly to resemble the provided screenshot, but adapted to Arata theme. I will also incorporate a "fun" vibe for the banner text "지금 가입만 해도! **무료이용권**을 드려요" and add the SNS text initials.


**Adding Event Handling**

19금 웹툰이랑 일반웹툰은 다른데

**Filtering Webtoon Content**

I'm currently focused on the `UnlimitedList` and `CoinPage` components. The goal is to filter the webtoon content they display based on the `isAdult` toggle within `ThemeContext`. This requires integrating the `isAdult` state with the content filtering logic in these components, which will determine what is presented to the user.


**Analyzing Displayed Webtoons**

I'm now diving deeper into `CoinPage.tsx`. It seems it doesn't have explicit filtering for `isAdult` across all its sections like `UnlimitedList` does. The user's comment is clear: I need to make sure the Coin Hall and Unlimited Webtoons fully respect the `isAdult` setting. Right now, I need to evaluate where and how the data for `CoinPage` is being populated, and whether its data sources mix adult content without explicit control based on the `isAdult` state.


**Revising Adult Content Logic**

I'm revisiting the adult content filtering, specifically how the `isAdult` toggle should behave. My analysis of `constants.tsx` confirms the mix of content. The user's comment, "19+ webtoons and general webtoons are different," is guiding my interpretation. I'm now considering stricter filtering in `UnlimitedList.tsx`, perhaps showing *only* adult content when the toggle is on, rather than everything. I need to make sure the app correctly implements an "all or nothing" logic based on the user's preference.


**Clarifying Content Filtering**

I've been thinking about the logic behind the `isAdult` flag. Right now, it looks like when `isAdult` is off, we hide adult content. I'm leaning toward making it a stricter filter. For example, when it's on, we show only adult webtoons, which might be the "Adult Mode" the user is familiar with. I'm focusing on `UnlimitedList.tsx` and `CoinPage.tsx` to ensure this strict filtering is applied consistently.


**Implementing Stricter Filtering**

I'm now implementing the strictest filtering logic based on the user's comments. My current approach involves treating `LATEST_WEBTOONS` as a mixed content pool. If `isAdult` is true, the system will now show only adult content, as suggested by the user's "general and 19+ are different" phrase. When `isAdult` is false, it won't. I'm taking the approach that I saw at the "benchmark site" - where the user's switch *totally* changes the content, which should satisfy the user.


**Adding Mock Adult Data**

I'm focusing on enriching the mock data in `constants.tsx` to support both filtering modes effectively. Currently, the dataset is insufficient for a good user experience in adult-only mode. I'm adding more items marked as `isAdult: true` to ensure the "19+" view is populated and reflects the user's expectations. This change will affect display on the home page as well, which is handled by `WebtoonGrid.tsx`.


**Updating Consistent Display**

I'm now focused on achieving consistency across the app, as the user requested. My plan involves modifying `WebtoonGrid.tsx` to align with the stricter filtering logic. Previously, I added more mock adult data to `constants.tsx`, and I'm updating `UnlimitedList.tsx`. The goal is to ensure the Home Page, Coin Hall and Unlimited Webtoons fully support this. The logic has been adjusted to make "Adult Mode" and "General Mode" the user's primary experience.


**Applying Filter Updates**

I'm now integrating the stricter filtering across all components. I'm modifying `components/WebtoonGrid.tsx` and verifying the filter logic. The goal is a unified user experience where the `isAdult` state dictates a clear content division, specifically between "adult-only" and a broader selection, exactly as the user requested. My focus is on ensuring all parts of the site reflect this change uniformly.

**Examining the Core Logic**

I've been analyzing the user's request, specifically identifying the desired goal: restricting the "19+ mode" toggle. My current focus is on the essential condition – the requirement for a logged-in user to activate the "19+" feature. This restriction seems key to the overall solution.


**Pinpointing the User Interaction**

I'm now zeroing in on the user experience. The initial behavior is unrestricted; the button flips instantly. The goal is to route the action. If the user's logged in, let the toggle function normally. If not, the click should launch the login modal instead. I've pinpointed `Header.tsx` as the primary component needing adjustment, leveraging its existing `isLoggedIn` state.


**Refining Implementation Strategy**

I'm now revising my approach. I've located the `toggleAdult` button handler within `Header.tsx` and will intercept its click event. The core logic involves checking the `isLoggedIn` state. If true, the `toggleAdult` function (obtained from `useTheme()`) will execute as normal. Otherwise, the click will trigger the `'login'` modal using the `authModal` state, a more suitable solution given the current setup. I've also verified that the changes specifically target the header component shown, as no toggle exists within `MobileBottomNav`.


**Finalizing Button Behavior**

I'm now implementing the click handler. I've opted for a more direct approach within `components/Header.tsx`. My focus is on the `handleAdultToggle` function, the new button behavior. I've adjusted the code to check the `isLoggedIn` state. If the user's not logged in and attempts to activate the 19+ feature (turning it on), the login modal appears using the `setAuthModal` state. Otherwise, turning it off is allowed.


**Addressing Logout Scenario**

I'm now focusing on a potential edge case: handling user logout. If a user is logged out while the "19+" feature is enabled, I'll need to disable it. I'll modify `Header.tsx` to ensure `isAdult` is reset to false upon logout, maintaining a secure and expected user experience. I've also verified that the changes will not be moved to ThemeContext.tsx.


**Refining Toggle Implementation**

My focus is now on the `Header.tsx` implementation, ensuring the logic precisely matches the requirements. I'm prioritizing the user's intent:  the "19+" feature can be disabled regardless of login status, but can only be *enabled* if a user is logged in. I'm also addressing the crucial logout scenario, ensuring the "19+" setting defaults to off, maintaining a secure user state. I am ensuring that the correct and concise logic is implemented within the new function `handleAdultToggle`.


**Optimizing Button Behavior**

I'm now integrating the user's login flow directly into the button's functionality, focusing on user experience. Following a successful login triggered via the modal, and given that the user wants to enable the 19+ feature, the "19 OFF" mode button should enable the "19 ON" mode. I've also verified this behavior with a quick mental check. I'll need to update the `handleLoginSuccess` function and the "19+" button.


**Validating Final Implementation**

I'm now implementing the final changes and verifying the integrity of the code. I've updated the button's `onClick` to trigger the new `handleAdultClick` function, and am confident that the logout flow is now secure. The logic ensures that turning off the "19+" feature remains unrestricted. I've also double-checked `MobileBottomNav` and can confirm that the toggle control is absent, so it doesn't need modification. The code changes are complete, and I'm confident they meet all requirements.


**Consolidating Modal Activation**

I'm now refining the logic in `Header.tsx`, focusing on the user's explicit directive:  "19금 온 하려면 로그인 해야해." Opening the login modal remains the core UX, as a toast or alert would require additional complexity. I've confirmed that directly opening the modal aligns with standard behavior for this feature. I have not included any additional alerts or toasts in this refactor. Furthermore, the `isLoggedIn` state will remain local to the header, which is standard for a frontend prototype.
